analysis.one_liner: Requires FDA to certify generic drugs as therapeutically equivalent and bars states from adding stricter requirements.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first subcommittee referral and received no cosponsors, no vote, and no action before Congress ended in 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the FDA, when it approves a generic drug, to make a formal finding of whether that generic is therapeutically equivalent to the brand-name original — the finding that lets pharmacies substitute the cheaper generic automatically [S2, S3]. It would spell out the criteria for equivalence: same active ingredients, same dose form and strength, same expected clinical effect and safety profile [S3]. It would also preempt state laws, barring states from imposing therapeutic-equivalence requirements that differ from or add to the federal standard [S2, S3]. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health subcommittee, where it died [S1, S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who fill prescriptions would benefit if cheaper generics could be substituted for brand-name drugs more readily, backed by a clear federal equivalence finding. Generic drug makers would gain from a standardized approval pathway that makes their products easier to substitute at the pharmacy counter.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Prescription drug patients and generic makers

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to state in every generic approval whether the drug is therapeutically equivalent to the brand-name drug, replacing ambiguity that can be used to block substitution [S3].
Defines therapeutic equivalence concretely: same active ingredients, dosage form, route, strength, standards, same expected clinical effect and safety, and no unresolved bioequivalence problem [S3].
Writes that equivalence finding into the Orange Book-style approval record, so pharmacists and state substitution laws can rely on a single federal determination [S3].
Prevents state or local governments from keeping nonconforming therapeutic-equivalence requirements that could delay generic drugs reaching patients [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the cost, since easier generic substitution erodes the period during which they can sell patent-protected drugs at premium prices. States would cede some authority over drug-equivalence rules to the federal government.

drawbacks.text: The federal preemption clause strips states of the ability to set stricter equivalence requirements than the FDA's, even where a state believes its standard better protects patients [S3].

A one-size-fits-all federal equivalence determination could override state substitution rules that were tailored to local pharmacy practice, and an error at the federal level would leave states no authority to correct it [S3].
The bill imposed new FDA approval duties without additional process, and it drew no cosponsors — no other member was willing to attach their name to the approach [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the upside is faster access to cheaper generics with a clear federal stamp of equivalence; the downside is losing state-level oversight as a backstop if the FDA's equivalence finding is wrong or too loose. The trade-off favors cheaper medicine but concentrates more power in one federal agency.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health subcommittee, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the Generic Drugs Access Act of 2005 on May 11, 2005 [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
On May 23, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where it sat with no markup, no vote, and no further action [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its lifetime [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, because a bill that would have formalized generic equivalence findings — easing substitution of cheaper copies of their drugs — never moved. State governments also keep their authority over equivalence rules that the bill would have preempted.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill with zero cosponsors from either party, and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record.

industries.note: A formal federal equivalence finding would make generic versions of their drugs easier to certify and substitute, cutting into premium-price sales. The bill's death preserves the status quo, in which ambiguity can slow generic uptake.
The bill would standardize how their products are judged equivalent to brand-name drugs, easing pharmacy substitution. Cheaper generics reaching patients is the same outcome patients want.

A clear federal equivalence determination would simplify substitution decisions, but the preemption of state rules could override substitution practices some states had tailored. The net effect on their operations is genuinely two-sided.

The bill bars states from keeping therapeutic-equivalence requirements that differ from or add to the federal standard, a direct loss of regulatory authority — though the federal standard it defers to is itself designed to assure safe, effective generics.
